title: AP Chemistry
description: Free AP Chemistry study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Atomic Structure & Moles

concepts.intro: Atoms are built from protons, neutrons, and electrons, and isotopes of an element differ only in neutron count.
b: Protons (+1, in nucleus) define the element via atomic number Z; neutrons (0, in nucleus) add mass; electrons (-1) occupy orbitals around the nucleus
Mass number A = protons + neutrons; isotopes have the same Z but different A
Atomic mass on the periodic table is a weighted average of all naturally occurring isotopes
Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons: cations (+) lose electrons, anions (-) gain electrons
Nuclear symbol notation: superscript = mass number, subscript = atomic number, e.g. carbon-14 is written with A=14, Z=6

concepts.intro: The mole is chemistry's counting unit, linking the atomic scale to measurable macroscopic quantities.
b: 1 mole = 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number, N_A)
Molar mass (g/mol) numerically equals the atomic/molecular mass in amu from the periodic table
moles = mass (g) / molar mass (g/mol); mass = moles x molar mass
number of particles = moles x 6.022 x 10^23
Molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of all atoms in its formula

concepts.intro: Mass spectrometry measures isotope masses and relative abundances, which are used to calculate an element's average atomic mass.
b: A mass spectrometer ionizes, accelerates, and deflects particles by mass-to-charge ratio to separate isotopes
Average atomic mass = sum of (isotope mass x fractional abundance) for all isotopes
Example: chlorine is ~75.77% Cl-35 (34.97 amu) and ~24.23% Cl-37 (36.97 amu), giving an average of about 35.45 amu
Peaks further right on a mass spectrum correspond to heavier isotopes; peak height/intensity corresponds to relative abundance

concepts.intro: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound; the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it.
b: To find an empirical formula from mass or % composition: convert to moles, divide by the smallest mole value, then convert to whole numbers
Molecular formula = empirical formula x n, where n = molar mass (molecular) / empirical formula mass
Percent composition of an element = (mass of element in 1 mole compound / molar mass of compound) x 100%
Combustion analysis of a hydrocarbon uses moles of CO2 produced to find moles of C, and moles of H2O to find moles of H

concepts.intro: Coulomb's law governs the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and electrons, underlying atomic size and ionization trends.
b: Coulomb's law: F is proportional to (q1 x q2)/r^2 — force increases with charge magnitude and decreases with the square of distance
Higher effective nuclear charge pulls electrons closer, shrinking atomic radius
Greater distance between nucleus and valence electrons (more shielding/energy levels) weakens attraction, easing ionization
This same law explains why removing successive electrons from an atom requires increasingly more energy

keyFacts: n = m/M (moles = mass / molar mass); particles = n x 6.022 x 10^23
Average atomic mass = Σ(isotope mass x fractional abundance)
Molecular formula = empirical formula x n, where n = (molar mass)/(empirical formula mass)
Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons; atomic number (Z) = protons = electrons in a neutral atom
traps: Atomic mass on the periodic table is a weighted average of isotopes, not the mass of any single atom
Molar mass and molecular mass have the same numeric value but different units (g/mol vs amu) — students often confuse them
An empirical formula is the simplest ratio; it is not necessarily the actual molecular formula unless n = 1
Isotopes of the same element have identical chemical behavior (same electron count) but different mass — mass differences don't change reactivity

units.name: Stoichiometry

concepts.intro: A balanced equation conserves atoms of each element and reflects the law of conservation of mass.
b: Balance by adjusting coefficients only, never subscripts (changing a subscript changes the substance's identity)
Balance elements that appear in only one reactant and one product first; balance free elements (like O2, H2) last
Check work by counting atoms of every element on both sides after balancing
Balanced coefficients give the mole ratios used in all stoichiometry calculations

concepts.intro: Balanced equation coefficients give exact mole ratios that convert between amounts of any two substances in a reaction.
b: General path: mass/volume of A -> moles of A -> moles of B (using mole ratio from balanced equation) -> mass/volume of B
Mole ratio = coefficient of desired substance / coefficient of given substance
For gases at STP, 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L
For solutions, moles = Molarity (mol/L) x Volume (L)

concepts.intro: The limiting reactant is used up first and determines the maximum theoretical amount of product; percent yield compares actual to theoretical.
b: To find the limiting reactant, calculate moles of product possible from each reactant — the one giving less product is limiting
Excess reactant is left over after the reaction goes to completion
Theoretical yield is the maximum product calculated from the limiting reactant
Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%
Percent yield is always less than or equal to 100% due to side reactions, impurities, or practical losses

concepts.intro: Molarity expresses solution concentration, and dilution calculations track moles of solute as volume changes.
b: Molarity (M) = moles of solute / liters of solution
Dilution equation: M1V1 = M2V2 (moles of solute stay constant when solvent is added)
To make a solution of known molarity, calculate moles needed, then mass needed via molar mass
Titration uses the equation moles acid = moles base at the equivalence point (for a 1:1 acid-base reaction) to find an unknown concentration

concepts.intro: Reactions are often classified by pattern, which helps predict products before balancing.
b: Synthesis: A + B -> AB; Decomposition: AB -> A + B
Single replacement: A + BC -> AC + B (predict using an activity series for metals)
Double replacement (often precipitation or acid-base): AB + CD -> AD + CB
Combustion of a hydrocarbon: CxHy + O2 -> CO2 + H2O
Net ionic equations omit spectator ions, showing only species that actually change in a reaction

keyFacts: Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%
M1V1 = M2V2 for dilutions; moles = M x V for solutions
The limiting reactant produces the least amount of product and is fully consumed
At STP, 1 mole of ideal gas = 22.4 L
traps: Mole ratios come from balanced coefficients, not from the masses or grams given in the problem — convert to moles first, not last
The reactant with the smaller mass or fewer grams is not automatically the limiting reactant — you must compare moles of product each could form
Percent yield over 100% signals an experimental error (like impure product), not a real result — it should be flagged, not accepted
Balancing equations changes coefficients, never subscripts — changing a subscript makes a different compound entirely

units.name: Gas Laws

concepts.intro: KMT models gases as particles in constant, random motion whose average kinetic energy depends only on temperature.
b: Gas particles are in constant, random, straight-line motion until they collide
Collisions between gas particles and container walls are perfectly elastic (no energy lost)
The volume of gas particles themselves is negligible compared to the container volume
Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature: KE_avg = (3/2)RT
There are no attractive or repulsive forces between ideal gas particles

concepts.intro: PV = nRT relates pressure, volume, moles, and temperature for an ideal gas in a single equation.
b: PV = nRT, where R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) (or 8.314 J/(mol·K) with SI units)
Temperature must always be converted to Kelvin: K = °C + 273
Can be rearranged to find molar mass: M = mRT/PV, or density: d = PM/RT
STP (standard conditions) is 0°C (273 K) and 1 atm, where 1 mole of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L

concepts.intro: Boyle's, Charles's, Gay-Lussac's, and the combined gas law describe relationships between two gas variables when others are held constant.
b: Boyle's Law (constant T, n): P1V1 = P2V2 — pressure and volume are inversely proportional
Charles's Law (constant P, n): V1/T1 = V2/T2 — volume and temperature are directly proportional
Gay-Lussac's Law (constant V, n): P1/T1 = P2/T2 — pressure and temperature are directly proportional
Combined gas law (constant n): P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2
Avogadro's Law (constant P, T): V1/n1 = V2/n2 — volume and moles are directly proportional

concepts.intro: Dalton's Law states that in a mixture of non-reacting gases, each gas contributes a partial pressure independent of the others.
b: Dalton's Law: P_total = P1 + P2 + P3 + ...
Partial pressure of a gas = mole fraction of that gas x total pressure: Pi = Xi x P_total
Mole fraction Xi = moles of gas i / total moles of gas
Common application: collecting gas over water requires subtracting water vapor pressure from total pressure to find the dry gas pressure

concepts.l: Effusion, Diffusion, and Real Gas Deviations
concepts.intro: Graham's Law describes how gas molar mass affects speed, while real gases deviate from ideal behavior at high pressure and low temperature.
b: Graham's Law: rate1/rate2 = sqrt(M2/M1) — lighter gases effuse/diffuse faster than heavier gases
Effusion is escape through a tiny hole; diffusion is gas spreading through space or another gas
Real gases deviate from ideal behavior most at high pressure (particle volume becomes significant) and low temperature (attractive forces become significant)
The van der Waals equation adds correction terms for intermolecular attraction (a) and particle volume (b) to the ideal gas law

keyFacts: PV = nRT, with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K); always convert temperature to Kelvin
P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 (combined gas law) when moles are constant
Graham's Law: rate1/rate2 = sqrt(M2/M1)
Dalton's Law: P_total = sum of partial pressures; Pi = Xi x P_total
traps: Temperature must be in Kelvin for all gas law calculations, not Celsius — forgetting this is the single most common gas law error
Real gases deviate most from ideal behavior at high pressure and low temperature, not at STP where ideal behavior is a good approximation
Lighter gases effuse faster, not slower — students often reverse Graham's Law's inverse square-root relationship
Ideal Gas Law assumes negligible particle volume and no intermolecular forces; these assumptions break down for real gases under extreme conditions

units.name: Thermochemistry

concepts.intro: Heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference, and specific heat capacity determines how much a substance's temperature changes for a given heat input.
b: q = mcΔT, where q = heat (J), m = mass (g), c = specific heat (J/g·°C), ΔT = T_final - T_initial
Specific heat of water is 4.18 J/(g·°C), unusually high, which is why water resists temperature change
Temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy; heat is energy transferred between objects at different temperatures
Heat flows spontaneously from a higher-temperature object to a lower-temperature object until thermal equilibrium is reached

concepts.intro: Calorimetry measures heat flow in physical or chemical processes, typically assuming heat lost by one substance equals heat gained by another.
b: In a coffee-cup calorimeter (constant pressure), q_reaction = -q_solution, and q_solution = mcΔT of the water/solution
Heat capacity of the calorimeter itself is often included in more precise calculations: q_cal = C_cal x ΔT
Bomb calorimeters measure heat at constant volume, giving ΔE (internal energy change) rather than ΔH directly
Molar enthalpy of reaction = q_reaction / moles of limiting reactant

concepts.intro: Enthalpy (H) is a state function, so Hess's Law allows ΔH for a reaction to be calculated by adding known steps regardless of path.
b: Hess's Law: if a reaction is the sum of steps, ΔH_total = sum of ΔH for each step
Reversing a reaction changes the sign of ΔH; multiplying a reaction by a factor multiplies ΔH by that factor
ΔH_rxn = Σ ΔHf°(products) - Σ ΔHf°(reactants), using standard enthalpies of formation
ΔHf° of an element in its standard state is defined as zero
Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0); endothermic reactions absorb heat (ΔH > 0)

concepts.intro: Enthalpy change can be estimated from the energy required to break bonds in reactants versus the energy released forming bonds in products.
b: ΔH_rxn ≈ Σ(bond energies broken, reactants) - Σ(bond energies formed, products)
Breaking bonds always requires energy input (endothermic); forming bonds always releases energy (exothermic)
This method gives an estimate because average bond energies vary slightly depending on molecular environment
A reaction is exothermic overall if more energy is released forming new bonds than was required to break old ones

concepts.l: Thermodynamics: Enthalpy, Entropy, and Gibbs Free Energy
concepts.intro: Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict whether a process is spontaneous at a given temperature.
b: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS (T in Kelvin); a negative ΔG indicates a spontaneous process
Entropy (S) is a measure of disorder/dispersal of energy; ΔS > 0 favors spontaneity, especially at high T
Four sign combinations: ΔH<0,ΔS>0 always spontaneous; ΔH>0,ΔS<0 never spontaneous; the other two combinations are temperature-dependent
Phase changes (solid→liquid→gas) increase entropy because molecular disorder and freedom of motion increase

keyFacts: q = mcΔT for heat transfer in a substance without phase change
ΔH_rxn = Σ ΔHf°(products) - Σ ΔHf°(reactants)
ΔG = ΔH - TΔS; ΔG < 0 means spontaneous
Hess's Law: ΔH values add when reaction steps are added; reversing a step flips the sign of ΔH
traps: Exothermic means the system releases energy (ΔH negative), but the surroundings get warmer, not colder — students often confuse which side loses energy
In calorimetry, q_reaction = -q_solution (opposite signs) because energy lost by one is gained by the other, not equal positive values
A reaction can be spontaneous even if endothermic, as long as ΔS is positive enough and T is high enough to make ΔG negative — spontaneity is not just about heat release
Bond breaking always costs energy and bond forming always releases energy; a common error is reversing which process is endothermic vs. exothermic

units.name: Atomic Structure & Periodicity

concepts.intro: Electrons fill orbitals in a predictable order set by energy, and this arrangement explains chemical behavior.
b: Aufbau principle: electrons fill lowest-energy orbitals first, following the order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p...
Pauli exclusion principle: each orbital holds at most 2 electrons, with opposite spins
Hund's rule: electrons fill degenerate (same-energy) orbitals singly before pairing up
Noble gas (condensed) notation abbreviates configurations, e.g. Cl is [Ne]3s^2 3p^5
Transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d electrons when forming cations, e.g. Fe -> Fe2+ removes two 4s electrons
Valence electrons (outermost s and p, plus d for transition metals) determine bonding and chemical properties

concepts.intro: Four quantum numbers uniquely describe each electron's energy, shape, orientation, and spin within an atom.
b: Principal quantum number n (1, 2, 3...) gives the energy level/shell size
Angular momentum number l (0 to n-1) gives the subshell shape: l=0 is s, l=1 is p, l=2 is d, l=3 is f
Magnetic quantum number m_l gives orbital orientation (e.g. p has 3 orbitals: px, py, pz)
Spin quantum number m_s is +1/2 or -1/2, describing the two possible electron spins in an orbital
s orbitals are spherical; p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along an axis; d orbitals have more complex cloverleaf shapes

concepts.intro: Atomic size changes predictably across periods and down groups due to nuclear charge and shielding.
b: Atomic radius decreases left to right across a period: increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons in with little added shielding
Atomic radius increases down a group: each row adds a new occupied shell, increasing distance from the nucleus
Cations are smaller than their parent atom (fewer electrons, same or more nuclear pull); anions are larger than their parent atom
Isoelectronic species (same electron count) shrink as nuclear charge increases, e.g. O2- > F- > Ne > Na+ > Mg2+
Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) is the net positive charge felt by valence electrons after accounting for shielding by inner electrons

concepts.intro: Ionization energy and electronegativity both generally increase toward fluorine, reflecting how tightly an atom holds electrons.
b: First ionization energy (IE1) is the energy to remove one electron from a gaseous atom; it increases across a period and decreases down a group
Successive ionization energies increase, with a large jump after removing all valence electrons (breaking into a stable core shell)
Exceptions: IE dips slightly from Group 2 to 13 (p orbital easier to remove than filled s) and from Group 15 to 16 (paired electron easier to remove than half-filled set)
Electronegativity measures an atom's pull on shared electrons in a bond; it increases across a period and decreases down a group
Fluorine is the most electronegative element; cesium/francium are among the least (most metallic/electropositive)
Electron affinity (energy change when an atom gains an electron) is generally most negative (most favorable) near the halogens

concepts.intro: PES experimentally measures the binding energies of electrons in different orbitals, providing direct evidence for electron configuration and shielding.
b: PES bombards atoms with high-energy photons, ejecting electrons; measuring their kinetic energy gives the binding energy of the orbital they came from
Higher binding energy = electrons held more tightly = closer to the nucleus or less shielded (core electrons > valence electrons)
A PES spectrum shows peaks at different binding energies; peak height (relative intensity) is proportional to the number of electrons in that orbital/subshell
Peaks cluster into groups matching shells; within a shell, s orbitals have higher binding energy than p (closer to nucleus, less shielded)
PES data can be used to identify unknown elements or confirm electron configurations from first principles

concepts.intro: Coulomb's law quantifies the electrostatic forces between charges and underlies most periodic trends and bonding.
b: Coulomb's law: F = k(q1 x q2)/r^2 — force is proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to the square of distance
Larger effective nuclear charge (more protons felt) means stronger attraction, higher ionization energy, and smaller radius
Greater distance between nucleus and valence electrons (larger n, more shielding) means weaker attraction, lower ionization energy, larger radius
Shielding (inner electrons blocking nuclear charge) reduces the effective pull felt by valence electrons
These same electrostatic principles explain why ionic bond strength (lattice energy) increases with higher charge and smaller ionic radius

keyFacts: Electron configurations fill in order of increasing energy (Aufbau) with Hund's rule maximizing unpaired spins in degenerate orbitals.
Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group; ionization energy and electronegativity show the opposite trend.
PES peak position = binding energy (closer to nucleus = higher); peak height = number of electrons in that orbital.
Effective nuclear charge and Coulomb's law (F = kq1q2/r^2) explain essentially every periodic trend.
traps: Transition metals lose 4s electrons first when ionizing, not 3d electrons — Fe2+ is [Ar]3d^6, not [Ar]4s^2 3d^4.
Ionization energy increases across a period and up a group, not down a group — don't mix up radius and IE directions.
PES peak height reflects the number of electrons in a subshell, not the energy — taller peaks mean more electrons, not more tightly bound.
Anions are larger, not smaller, than their neutral parent atom because added electron-electron repulsion outweighs the same nuclear charge.

units.name: Bonding & IMFs

concepts.intro: The three major bonding types arise from different ways atoms share or transfer electrons, driven by electronegativity differences.
b: Ionic bonds form via electron transfer between a metal and nonmetal, creating a lattice of oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction
Covalent bonds form via electron sharing between nonmetals; can be nonpolar (equal sharing, same/similar electronegativity) or polar (unequal sharing)
Metallic bonding involves a 'sea of delocalized electrons' around a lattice of metal cations, explaining conductivity, malleability, and ductility
Bond polarity is judged by electronegativity difference: ~0 is nonpolar covalent, ~0.4-1.7 is polar covalent, >1.7 is generally ionic (rule of thumb)
Lattice energy (ionic bond strength) increases with higher ionic charge and smaller ionic radius, per Coulomb's law
Network covalent solids (e.g. diamond, SiO2) have covalent bonds throughout, giving very high melting points and hardness

concepts.intro: Lewis structures show how valence electrons are arranged as bonds and lone pairs, with formal charge helping choose the best structure.
b: Count total valence electrons, place atoms with least electronegative (usually) in center, connect with single bonds, then distribute remaining electrons as lone pairs to satisfy octets
Formal charge = (valence electrons) - (nonbonding electrons) - (1/2 bonding electrons); the best Lewis structure minimizes formal charges, with negative charges on more electronegative atoms
Resonance structures occur when multiple valid Lewis structures differ only in electron placement (e.g. ozone, nitrate); the real structure is an average (resonance hybrid)
Expanded octets are possible for period 3+ elements (e.g. S, P) using available d-orbitals or higher orbital availability, e.g. SF6, PCl5
Exceptions to the octet rule include odd-electron species (NO, NO2), electron-deficient atoms (BF3, B has 6 electrons), and expanded octets

concepts.intro: VSEPR theory predicts 3D molecular shape from the number of electron domains (bonds + lone pairs) around a central atom, which repel each other to minimize energy.
b: 2 domains: linear (180 degrees), e.g. CO2; 3 domains: trigonal planar (120 degrees), e.g. BF3, or bent (~120) with 1 lone pair, e.g. SO2
4 domains: tetrahedral (109.5 degrees), e.g. CH4; trigonal pyramidal with 1 lone pair, e.g. NH3; bent with 2 lone pairs, e.g. H2O
5 domains: trigonal bipyramidal (90/120 degrees), e.g. PCl5; seesaw (1 lone pair), T-shaped (2 lone pairs), linear (3 lone pairs)
6 domains: octahedral (90 degrees), e.g. SF6; square pyramidal (1 lone pair); square planar (2 lone pairs)
Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles slightly below ideal (e.g. H2O is ~104.5 degrees, not 109.5)
Hybridization matches electron domain count: 2 domains = sp, 3 = sp2, 4 = sp3, 5 = sp3d, 6 = sp3d2

concepts.intro: A molecule's overall polarity depends on both individual bond polarities and molecular geometry, since bond dipoles can cancel by symmetry.
b: A polar bond contributes a bond dipole pointing toward the more electronegative atom
A molecule is nonpolar if bond dipoles cancel by symmetry, even with polar bonds (e.g. CO2, CCl4, BF3)
A molecule is polar if bond dipoles do not cancel, often due to lone pairs or asymmetry (e.g. H2O, NH3, CHCl3)
Symmetric molecules with identical terminal atoms and no lone pairs on the central atom (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) tend to be nonpolar
Molecular polarity determines solubility ('like dissolves like') and physical properties like boiling point

concepts.intro: Intermolecular forces are attractions between separate molecules, weaker than covalent/ionic bonds, but they govern boiling points, solubility, and physical states.
b: London dispersion forces (LDFs) exist between all molecules/atoms, from temporary induced dipoles; strength increases with more electrons and larger surface area
Dipole-dipole forces occur between polar molecules, from permanent partial charges attracting oppositely charged ends of neighboring molecules
Hydrogen bonding is an especially strong dipole-dipole interaction when H is bonded directly to N, O, or F, which then attracts a lone pair on N/O/F of another molecule
Relative strength: ionic/covalent bonds > hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole > London dispersion (for similar-sized molecules)
Stronger IMFs lead to higher boiling/melting points, higher viscosity, and lower vapor pressure
Water's unusually high boiling point, surface tension, and the fact that ice floats are all consequences of extensive hydrogen bonding

concepts.intro: The type of particle and force holding a solid together determines its physical properties, and phase diagrams map how substances change state with temperature and pressure.
b: Ionic solids: hard, brittle, high melting point, conduct electricity only when molten/dissolved (e.g. NaCl)
Metallic solids: malleable, ductile, conduct electricity as solids (delocalized electrons), wide range of melting points
Molecular solids: held by IMFs (LDF, dipole-dipole, H-bonding); generally soft with low melting points, do not conduct electricity
Network covalent (atomic) solids: extremely hard, very high melting points, generally do not conduct (except graphite) (e.g. diamond, quartz)
Phase diagrams plot pressure vs. temperature, showing solid/liquid/gas regions separated by phase-boundary curves that meet at the triple point

keyFacts: Bond type follows electronegativity difference: metal + nonmetal = ionic; nonmetal + nonmetal = covalent (polar or nonpolar).
VSEPR shape depends on total electron domains (bonding + lone pairs); lone pairs compress bond angles below the ideal.
IMF strength ranking: ionic/covalent bonds > hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole > London dispersion forces.
A molecule can have polar bonds yet be nonpolar overall if the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry (e.g. CO2, CCl4).
traps: A molecule with polar bonds is not automatically polar — check geometry, since symmetric shapes cancel dipoles (CO2 is nonpolar despite polar C=O bonds).
Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded directly to N, O, or F — an O-H bond elsewhere in a molecule counts, but C-H bonds never count as hydrogen bonding.
London dispersion forces exist in ALL molecules, not just nonpolar ones — they're often the dominant force in large nonpolar molecules, sometimes stronger than dipole-dipole in smaller polar ones.

Lone pairs count as electron domains for determining shape (VSEPR), but they are not counted when naming the molecular geometry itself (e.g. NH3 is 'trigonal pyramidal,' not 'tetrahedral,' despite 4 domains).

units.name: Kinetics & Equilibrium

concepts.intro: Reaction rate measures how fast reactants are consumed or products form, and the rate law expresses this mathematically in terms of concentrations.
b: Rate = -(1/a)[d[A]/dt] = (1/b)[d[B]/dt]... using stoichiometric coefficients to relate rates of different species
Rate law: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where m and n are reaction orders determined experimentally (NOT from stoichiometric coefficients)
Overall reaction order = sum of individual orders (m + n); k is the rate constant, specific to a reaction at a given temperature
Method of initial rates: compare experiments where one concentration changes while others are held constant to solve for each order
Zero order: rate is independent of [A] (rate = k); first order: rate is proportional to [A]; second order: rate is proportional to [A]^2
Units of k depend on overall order: M/s for zero order, 1/s for first order, 1/(M*s) for second order

concepts.intro: Integrated rate laws relate concentration directly to time, letting you predict concentration at any point or determine reaction order from a graph.
b: Zero order: [A] = [A]0 - kt; a plot of [A] vs. t is linear
First order: ln[A] = ln[A]0 - kt (or ln([A]0/[A]) = kt); a plot of ln[A] vs. t is linear
Second order: 1/[A] = 1/[A]0 + kt; a plot of 1/[A] vs. t is linear
Half-life (t1/2) for first order is constant: t1/2 = 0.693/k, independent of concentration
Zero-order half-life decreases over time ([A]0/2k); second-order half-life increases over time (1/(k[A]0))
Graphing concentration data in these three ways (linear, ln, 1/[A]) and finding which gives a straight line reveals the reaction order

concepts.intro: Reactions occur when molecules collide with sufficient energy and correct orientation, and most reactions proceed through a multi-step mechanism.
b: Collision theory: reaction rate depends on collision frequency, energy (must exceed activation energy Ea), and proper orientation
Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum energy needed for a collision to result in reaction; a catalyst lowers Ea by providing an alternate pathway
A reaction mechanism is a series of elementary steps that sum to the overall reaction; intermediates are produced then consumed (don't appear in overall equation)
The rate-determining step (slowest step) determines the overall rate law; for an elementary step, the rate law can be written directly from its stoichiometry
A valid mechanism must sum to the overall balanced equation and produce a rate law consistent with the experimentally observed one
Catalysts increase rate without being consumed; they appear in an early step and are regenerated in a later step

concepts.intro: Equilibrium is a dynamic state where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, and Keq quantifies the ratio of products to reactants at that point.
b: At equilibrium, forward rate = reverse rate, so concentrations (not necessarily equal) remain constant over time
Keq = [products]^coefficients / [reactants]^coefficients, using equilibrium concentrations; pure solids and liquids are omitted
Kc uses concentrations; Kp uses partial pressures for gases, related by Kp = Kc(RT)^(delta n)
Large K (>>1) favors products at equilibrium; small K (<<1) favors reactants; K near 1 means comparable amounts of both
Reaction quotient Q has the same form as K but uses current (non-equilibrium) concentrations; if Q < K reaction shifts forward, if Q > K it shifts reverse, if Q = K it's at equilibrium
ICE tables (Initial, Change, Equilibrium) organize concentration changes to solve for equilibrium concentrations or K

concepts.intro: Le Chatelier's principle predicts how an equilibrium system responds to a disturbance by shifting to partially counteract the change.
b: Adding a reactant (or removing a product) shifts equilibrium toward products (forward); the reverse shifts it toward reactants
Increasing volume/decreasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward the side with more moles of gas; decreasing volume/increasing pressure shifts toward fewer moles of gas
Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not shift equilibrium (partial pressures/concentrations of reactants and products are unchanged)
Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction; decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction (treat heat as a reactant or product)
Changing temperature is the only disturbance that actually changes the value of K; changing concentration, pressure, or volume shifts the position but K stays the same
Catalysts speed up the approach to equilibrium (both directions equally) but do not shift its position or change K

concepts.intro: Gibbs free energy determines reaction spontaneity and connects thermodynamics to the equilibrium constant.
b: Delta G = Delta H - T*Delta S; a reaction is spontaneous (favorable) when Delta G < 0
Delta G < 0: exergonic/spontaneous as written; Delta G > 0: nonspontaneous as written (spontaneous in reverse); Delta G = 0: at equilibrium
Delta G° relates to K by Delta G° = -RT ln(K); large K corresponds to very negative Delta G°
Delta G = Delta G° + RT ln(Q) describes free energy under non-standard conditions, showing how a reaction proceeds toward equilibrium (Q approaches K)
Temperature can flip spontaneity when Delta H and Delta S have the same sign (e.g. endothermic but entropy-increasing reactions become spontaneous at high T)

keyFacts: Rate laws (rate = k[A]^m[B]^n) are determined experimentally, never from the balanced equation's coefficients.
First-order half-life is constant (t1/2 = 0.693/k); zero- and second-order half-lives change with concentration.
Only a temperature change alters the value of K; concentration, pressure/volume, and catalysts shift the equilibrium position but not K itself.
Delta G° = -RT ln(K): a very negative Delta G° corresponds to a very large K, and Delta G = 0 exactly at equilibrium.
traps: Reaction order comes from experimental data (initial rates method), not from the stoichiometric coefficients in the balanced equation.
Adding an inert gas at constant volume does NOT shift equilibrium, because it doesn't change any reactant/product concentration or partial pressure.
A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally — it changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached, not the equilibrium position or K.
Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium based on which direction is endothermic, not simply 'always toward products' — treat heat as a reactant (endothermic) or product (exothermic).

units.name: Acids-Bases & Electrochemistry

concepts.intro: Acids and bases can be defined by proton or electron transfer, and pH/pOH provide a convenient scale for describing [H+] and [OH-].
b: Bronsted-Lowry: acids donate H+ (protons), bases accept H+; Lewis: acids accept electron pairs, bases donate electron pairs
pH = -log[H+]; pOH = -log[OH-]; pH + pOH = 14.00 at 25°C (from Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14)
Neutral: pH = 7; acidic: pH < 7; basic: pH > 7 (at 25°C)
Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4) and strong bases (Group 1/2 hydroxides) dissociate 100% in water
For strong acids/bases, [H+] or [OH-] equals the given concentration directly (accounting for stoichiometry, e.g. Ca(OH)2 gives 2x [OH-])
Conjugate acid-base pairs differ by one H+ (e.g. NH4+/NH3, HCO3-/CO3^2-); the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base

concepts.intro: Weak acids and bases only partially dissociate in water, and Ka/Kb quantify the extent of that ionization at equilibrium.
b: Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA] for HA <-> H+ + A-; larger Ka means a stronger (more dissociated) weak acid
Kb = [BH+][OH-]/[B] for B + H2O <-> BH+ + OH-; larger Kb means a stronger weak base
Ka x Kb = Kw = 1.0 x 10^-14 for a conjugate acid-base pair (pKa + pKb = 14)
For a weak acid, use an ICE table with x = [H+] and the approximation x << [HA]0 (valid when Ka is small relative to concentration)
Percent ionization = ([H+]/[HA]0) x 100%; percent ionization increases as initial concentration decreases (more dilute = more dissociated)
pKa = -log(Ka); a lower pKa means a stronger acid

concepts.intro: Buffers resist changes in pH by containing both a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid) in significant amounts.
b: A buffer is made from a weak acid/conjugate base pair (or weak base/conjugate acid pair) present in comparable amounts
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); useful for finding buffer pH or the ratio needed for a target pH
Buffer capacity is greatest when [A-] = [HA] (pH = pKa), and buffers work best within about 1 pH unit of pKa
Adding acid to a buffer: H+ reacts with the conjugate base (A-); adding base: OH- reacts with the weak acid (HA); the buffer components adjust to absorb the change
Buffers are used in blood (carbonic acid/bicarbonate), biological systems, and lab solutions to maintain stable pH

concepts.intro: Titrations use a solution of known concentration to determine the concentration or identity of an unknown acid or base, tracked via a pH curve.
b: Equivalence point: moles of acid = moles of base (accounting for stoichiometry); this is where the titration curve has its steepest rise (inflection point)
Strong acid + strong base titration: equivalence point pH = 7
Weak acid + strong base titration: equivalence point pH > 7 (conjugate base of the weak acid makes the solution basic)
Weak base + strong acid titration: equivalence point pH < 7 (conjugate acid makes the solution acidic)
Half-equivalence point (half of the acid neutralized): pH = pKa for a weak acid titration, since [HA] = [A-] there
Indicators change color near their own pKa; choose an indicator whose color-change range brackets the equivalence point pH
Titration curves for polyprotic acids show multiple equivalence points, one for each ionizable proton

concepts.intro: Oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions involve electron transfer, tracked using oxidation numbers and balanced with half-reactions.
b: Oxidation = loss of electrons (oxidation number increases); reduction = gain of electrons (oxidation number decreases) — 'OIL RIG'
The oxidizing agent is reduced (it causes oxidation of something else); the reducing agent is oxidized (it causes reduction of something else)
Assign oxidation numbers: free elements = 0; monatomic ions = ion charge; O is usually -2; H is usually +1; sum of oxidation numbers = overall charge
Balance redox equations using half-reactions: separate oxidation and reduction, balance atoms then charge (add electrons), then combine so electrons cancel
In acidic solution, balance O with H2O and H with H+; in basic solution, balance as if acidic, then add OH- to both sides to neutralize H+

concepts.intro: Galvanic cells convert spontaneous redox reactions into electrical energy, with standard reduction potentials predicting voltage and spontaneity.
b: In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode (negative electrode) and reduction occurs at the cathode (positive electrode) — 'AN OX, RED CAT'
Electrons flow through the external wire from anode to cathode; a salt bridge maintains charge neutrality by allowing ion flow between half-cells
E°cell = E°cathode(reduction) - E°anode(reduction), using standard reduction potentials from a table; a positive E°cell means a spontaneous reaction
Delta G° = -nFE°cell, linking cell potential to free energy (n = moles of electrons transferred, F = Faraday's constant, 96,485 C/mol)
The Nernst equation, E = E° - (RT/nF)ln(Q), gives cell potential under non-standard conditions; at 25°C this simplifies to E = E° - (0.0592/n)log(Q)
Electrolytic cells use an external power source to force a nonspontaneous redox reaction to occur (opposite of galvanic cells, but same electrode naming: oxidation at anode, reduction at cathode)

keyFacts: pH + pOH = 14.00 at 25°C; Ka x Kb = Kw = 1.0 x 10^-14 for a conjugate acid-base pair.
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); buffers work best when pH is within about 1 unit of pKa.
At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration, pH = pKa; strong acid-strong base equivalence point is pH 7.
Galvanic cells: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode, electrons flow anode to cathode, and a positive E°cell means a spontaneous reaction.
traps: A weak acid-strong base titration has an equivalence point pH greater than 7, not 7 — don't assume every equivalence point is neutral.
Ka and Kb are related by Ka x Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair, not Ka = Kb — a stronger acid always has a weaker conjugate base.

In a galvanic cell, electrons flow from anode to cathode through the wire, while conventional current and cations in the salt bridge move to maintain charge balance — don't reverse anode/cathode with electrode charge sign.
Oxidation is loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number), not gain — mixing up OIL RIG is one of the most common redox errors.

quiz.q: What is the full electron configuration of chlorine (Z=17)?
quiz.e: Cl has 17 electrons: 2+2+6+2+5 = 17, giving 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5.

quiz.q: What is the condensed (noble-gas) electron configuration of Fe2+ (Z=26)?
quiz.e: Transition metals lose 4s electrons first when forming cations, so Fe2+ is [Ar]3d6, not [Ar]4s2 3d4.

quiz.q: Which principle states that electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly before pairing up?
quiz.e: Hund's rule minimizes electron-electron repulsion by keeping electrons unpaired in degenerate orbitals as long as possible.

quiz.q: According to the Pauli exclusion principle, how many electrons can occupy a single orbital?
quiz.e: Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons, and they must have opposite (paired) spins.

quiz.q: Which quantum number determines the shape of an orbital?
quiz.e: l determines subshell shape: l=0 is s (spherical), l=1 is p (dumbbell), l=2 is d.

quiz.q: Which element has the largest atomic radius?
quiz.e: Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period; Cs is in period 6, group 1, giving it the largest radius among these.

quiz.q: Which trend correctly describes atomic radius across period 3 (Na to Ar)?
o: Radius decreases due to increasing effective nuclear charge
Radius increases due to increasing effective nuclear charge
Radius increases due to added shielding
quiz.e: Across a period, protons are added with little added shielding, so effective nuclear charge increases and pulls electrons in, shrinking radius.

quiz.q: Rank these in order of increasing radius: Mg2+, Na+, F-, O2- (all isoelectronic with Ne).
quiz.e: For isoelectronic species, radius decreases as nuclear charge (proton count) increases; Mg2+ has the most protons (12) so it's smallest, O2- the fewest (8) so it's largest.

quiz.q: Why is the first ionization energy of aluminum lower than that of magnesium?
o: Al's valence electron is in a 3p orbital, which is higher energy and more easily removed than Mg's paired 3s electron
Al has fewer protons than Mg
Al has a larger atomic radius than Mg
quiz.e: The 3p electron in Al is slightly higher in energy and better shielded by the 3s electrons, making it easier to remove despite Al having one more proton.

quiz.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
quiz.e: Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the periodic table.

quiz.q: What happens to successive ionization energies of an atom?
o: They increase, with a large jump when a core (inner shell) electron must be removed
quiz.e: Removing electrons closer to the nucleus becomes progressively harder, with a big jump once all valence electrons are gone and the next electron is a stable core electron.

quiz.q: In a photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) spectrum, what does peak height represent?
o: The binding energy of the electrons
The relative number of electrons in that orbital/subshell
The atomic number of the element
quiz.e: Peak height (intensity) is proportional to the number of electrons occupying that orbital/subshell; peak position indicates binding energy.

quiz.q: In a PES spectrum, which peak corresponds to the highest binding energy?
o: The valence electrons, farthest from the nucleus
The core (1s) electrons, closest to the nucleus and least shielded
There is no difference between peaks
quiz.e: Core electrons are held most tightly (closest to the nucleus, least shielded), giving them the highest binding energy in a PES spectrum.

quiz.q: Which best explains why ionization energy generally decreases down a group?
o: Valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons
quiz.e: Down a group, added electron shells increase the average distance from the nucleus and increase shielding, both of which reduce the pull on valence electrons.

quiz.q: How many total electrons can the n=3 principal energy level hold?
quiz.e: n=3 has subshells 3s (2e), 3p (6e), 3d (10e), totaling 18 electrons (2n^2 = 2(3)^2 = 18).

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly ranks orbitals by increasing binding energy in a PES spectrum for a period-2 element?
quiz.e: Binding energy decreases with distance from the nucleus and increased shielding; valence 2p electrons have the lowest binding energy, core 1s the highest.

quiz.q: According to Coulomb's law, how does force between two charges change if the distance between them doubles?
quiz.e: F is proportional to 1/r^2, so doubling r reduces the force to (1/2)^2 = 1/4 of its original value.

quiz.q: Why does electron affinity become more negative (more favorable) moving toward the halogens?
o: Halogens have a strong pull for one more electron to complete a stable octet
Halogens have the largest atomic radius
Halogens have full valence shells already
quiz.e: Halogens need only one more electron to achieve a noble gas configuration, so they release a large amount of energy (very negative EA) when gaining an electron.

quiz.q: Which set of quantum numbers is NOT allowed for an electron?
quiz.e: For n=1, l can only be 0 (since l ranges from 0 to n-1); l=1 is not allowed when n=1.

quiz.q: Which best describes the relationship between effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) and periodic trends?
o: Higher Z_eff across a period increases ionization energy and electronegativity while decreasing atomic radius
Z_eff only affects atomic radius, not ionization energy
Z_eff is constant across a period
quiz.e: As Z_eff increases across a period, valence electrons are held more tightly, raising IE and electronegativity and shrinking radius.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the 3p subshell?
quiz.e: A p subshell has 3 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 6.

quiz.q: Which element is expected to have the smallest first ionization energy?
quiz.e: Francium is at the bottom-left of the periodic table, farthest from fluorine, giving it the lowest ionization energy of these options.

quiz.q: Why do noble gases have very high (large positive) first ionization energies?
o: Their filled valence shells are especially stable and resist electron removal
They have very large atomic radii
They have low effective nuclear charge
quiz.e: A completely filled valence shell is a low-energy, stable configuration, so removing an electron from it requires unusually high energy.

quiz.q: What is the shorthand (noble-gas) electron configuration for sulfur (Z=16)?
quiz.e: Sulfur has 16 electrons; after [Ne] (10 electrons), 6 remain: 3s2 3p4.

quiz.q: Which best describes why the second ionization energy of sodium is dramatically larger than its first?
o: The second electron must be removed from a stable, full inner shell after the single valence electron is gone
The second ionization energy is always similar to the first
Sodium becomes a nonmetal after first ionization
quiz.e: After removing its one valence electron, Na+ has a stable noble-gas core; removing a second electron from that filled shell requires far more energy.

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly lists sublevels in order of increasing energy for a multi-electron atom?
quiz.e: Due to the (n+l) filling order, 4s fills before 3d, and 3d fills before 4p in multi-electron atoms.

quiz.q: What is the term for the phenomenon where inner electrons reduce the nuclear charge experienced by outer electrons?
quiz.e: Shielding describes how core electrons block some of the nuclear attraction that would otherwise be felt by valence electrons.

quiz.q: A PES spectrum for an unknown element shows exactly four peaks with relative areas 2:2:6:2 (in order of increasing binding energy). What element is most consistent with this pattern?
quiz.e: Peak areas 2:2:6:2 match the subshells 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 — magnesium's electron configuration.

quiz.q: Which statement about electronegativity trends is correct?
o: Electronegativity generally increases across a period and decreases down a group
Electronegativity generally decreases across a period and increases down a group
Electronegativity is unrelated to atomic radius
Electronegativity is highest for noble gases
quiz.e: Electronegativity rises toward fluorine (across a period, up a group) because smaller atoms with higher Z_eff attract shared electrons more strongly.

quiz.q: Which best explains the exception where oxygen has a slightly lower first ionization energy than nitrogen?
o: Removing one electron from oxygen's paired 2p orbital relieves electron-electron repulsion, making it easier to remove than nitrogen's half-filled, more stable set
Oxygen has fewer protons than nitrogen
Oxygen has a larger atomic radius than nitrogen
quiz.e: Nitrogen's half-filled 2p3 configuration is extra stable; oxygen's 2p4 has one paired orbital, and removing that paired electron is easier due to repulsion, lowering its IE slightly below nitrogen's.

quiz.q: How many valence electrons does a phosphorus atom (Z=15) have?
quiz.e: Phosphorus is in group 15, with configuration [Ne]3s2 3p3, giving 5 valence electrons (2+3).

quiz.q: Which best describes how atomic radius changes when comparing a neutral atom to its cation?
o: The cation is smaller because it has fewer electrons and often a smaller occupied shell
The cation is larger because it has fewer electrons and less repulsion
The cation and atom are the same size
The cation is always larger due to increased nuclear attraction
quiz.e: Removing electrons decreases electron-electron repulsion and often removes an entire outer shell, making cations smaller than their parent atoms.

quiz.q: A student measures the ionization energies of an unknown element and finds a huge jump between the 2nd and 3rd ionization energies. What is the most likely number of valence electrons?
quiz.e: A large jump after the 2nd ionization energy suggests the 3rd electron must come from a stable, full inner shell, meaning the element has 2 valence electrons.

quiz.q: Which correctly identifies the group of the periodic table with the highest electron affinities (most exothermic)?
quiz.e: Halogens gain an electron very favorably (highly exothermic) because it completes their valence octet.

quiz.q: Which quantum number can take on values from -l to +l?
quiz.e: m_l describes orbital orientation and ranges in integer steps from -l to +l.

quiz.q: Why is it that as you move from left to right across period 4 through the transition metals, atomic radius changes relatively little compared to main-group elements?
o: Electrons are added to inner (n-1)d orbitals, which shield outer 4s electrons from the increasing nuclear charge fairly effectively
Transition metals have no valence electrons
Nuclear charge does not increase across the transition metals
Transition metals are all the same size by definition
quiz.e: Added electrons go into the d subshell (an inner shell), shielding the outer s electrons and largely offsetting the increasing nuclear charge, so radius stays fairly constant.

quiz.q: What does a large negative electron affinity indicate about an atom?
o: The atom releases a large amount of energy when it gains an electron, meaning it readily forms an anion
The atom requires a large amount of energy to gain an electron
The atom cannot form an anion
The atom has a very large radius
quiz.e: Electron affinity is defined as the energy change upon adding an electron; a large negative value means a large amount of energy is released, favoring anion formation.

quiz.q: Which correctly compares the sizes of Cl and Cl-?
o: Cl- is larger than Cl because the added electron increases electron-electron repulsion without adding nuclear charge
Cl- is smaller than Cl because it has one more proton
Cl and Cl- are the same size
Cl is larger than Cl- because anions always shrink
quiz.e: Adding an electron to form Cl- increases repulsion among the electrons while the nuclear charge stays the same, causing the electron cloud to expand.

quiz.q: A photoelectron spectrum for an element shows exactly two binding-energy peaks with equal peak areas (2:2). What is the most likely identity of this element?
quiz.e: Two equal-area peaks correspond to 1s2 2s2 — beryllium's electron configuration, with 2 electrons in each of its two occupied subshells.

quiz.q: Which best describes why potassium (Z=19) has an electron configuration of [Ar]4s1 rather than [Ar]3d1?
o: The 4s orbital is lower in energy than 3d for potassium, so it fills first per the Aufbau principle
3d orbitals do not exist for potassium
4s and 3d are always identical in energy
quiz.e: For elements around potassium and calcium, the 4s orbital is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills before 3d begins, giving [Ar]4s1 for potassium.

quiz.q: Which type of bond forms between sodium and chlorine?
quiz.e: A metal (Na) and a nonmetal (Cl) with a large electronegativity difference transfer electrons to form an ionic bond.

quiz.q: What is the electron-domain geometry and molecular shape of NH3?
o: Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, trigonal pyramidal molecular shape
Trigonal planar electron-domain geometry, trigonal planar molecular shape
Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, tetrahedral molecular shape
Trigonal pyramidal electron-domain geometry, trigonal pyramidal molecular shape
quiz.e: NH3 has 4 electron domains (3 bonds + 1 lone pair), giving tetrahedral electron geometry but trigonal pyramidal molecular shape because the lone pair isn't counted in the shape name.

quiz.q: Why is CO2 a nonpolar molecule even though the C=O bonds are polar?
o: The molecule is linear and symmetric, so the two bond dipoles cancel
Carbon and oxygen have the same electronegativity
CO2 has no lone pairs on carbon
CO2 does not have polar bonds
quiz.e: CO2 is linear with two identical, oppositely directed C=O bond dipoles that cancel exactly, making the molecule nonpolar overall.

quiz.q: Which intermolecular force is present in ALL molecules and atoms, polar or nonpolar?
quiz.e: London dispersion forces arise from temporary induced dipoles and are present in every atom or molecule, regardless of polarity.

quiz.q: Which of these substances can form hydrogen bonds with itself?
quiz.e: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded directly to N, O, or F; water (H-O-H) meets this requirement.

quiz.q: Why does water have an unusually high boiling point compared to other molecules of similar molar mass?
o: Water molecules experience extensive hydrogen bonding
Water has a very large molar mass
quiz.e: Water's O-H bonds allow extensive hydrogen bonding between molecules, requiring much more energy to separate them than expected from molar mass alone.

quiz.q: What is the hybridization of the central atom in a molecule with a trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry?
quiz.e: 5 electron domains correspond to sp3d hybridization and trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry.

quiz.q: Which best describes metallic bonding?
o: A lattice of metal cations surrounded by a sea of delocalized electrons
Discrete molecules held by covalent bonds
Ions held together by electrostatic attraction in a rigid lattice
Electron sharing between two identical nonmetal atoms
quiz.e: Metallic bonding involves delocalized valence electrons free to move throughout a lattice of metal cations, explaining conductivity and malleability.

quiz.q: A Lewis structure gives a central atom a formal charge of +1 while an alternative structure gives it a formal charge of 0, with all other formal charges equal. Which is generally the better structure?
o: The one with formal charge 0 on the central atom
The one with formal charge +1 on the central atom
quiz.e: The best Lewis structure minimizes formal charges as close to zero as possible.

quiz.q: Which pair of molecules would you expect to have the strongest London dispersion forces between molecules?
quiz.e: London dispersion forces increase with molecular size (more electrons, greater surface area); C8H18 (octane) is the largest molecule listed.

quiz.q: Rank these intermolecular forces from strongest to weakest for comparably sized molecules.
quiz.e: Hydrogen bonding is the strongest IMF (a special, strong case of dipole-dipole), followed by general dipole-dipole forces, then London dispersion forces.

quiz.q: What shape does a molecule with 4 bonding domains and 0 lone pairs on the central atom adopt?
quiz.e: With 4 bonding domains and no lone pairs, VSEPR predicts a tetrahedral molecular shape (e.g. CH4), with 109.5-degree bond angles.

quiz.q: Which best explains why the H-O-H bond angle in water (104.5 degrees) is smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle (109.5 degrees)?
o: The two lone pairs on oxygen repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle
Oxygen is too electronegative to allow 109.5 degrees
Hydrogen atoms repel each other strongly
quiz.e: Lone pair-bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion, pushing the two O-H bonds closer together than the ideal tetrahedral angle.

quiz.q: Which type of solid is expected to be extremely hard with an extremely high melting point due to a continuous network of covalent bonds?
quiz.e: Network covalent solids like diamond and quartz have covalent bonds extending throughout the entire structure, giving very high melting points and hardness.

quiz.q: What is the formal charge on nitrogen in NH4+ (nitrogen bonded to four hydrogens, no lone pairs)?
quiz.e: FC = 5 (valence e-) - 0 (nonbonding) - 1/2(8 bonding) = 5 - 0 - 4 = +1.

quiz.q: Which molecule is polar?
quiz.e: CHCl3 (chloroform) is tetrahedral but asymmetric (different atoms attached), so the bond dipoles do not cancel, making it polar.

quiz.q: What best describes resonance structures?
o: Multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule that differ only in electron placement, with the true structure being an average of all of them
Structures that show the molecule changing shape over time
Structures with different numbers of atoms
Isomers of a molecule with different molecular formulas
quiz.e: Resonance structures represent the same connectivity of atoms but different placements of electrons; the actual molecule is a hybrid/average of all resonance forms.

quiz.q: Why can sulfur in SF6 have an expanded octet (12 electrons around it)?
o: Sulfur is a period-3 element with accessible energy levels that allow more than 8 electrons around it
Sulfur always follows the octet rule strictly
Fluorine donates extra electrons to sulfur only
SF6 does not actually have an expanded octet
quiz.e: Elements in period 3 and beyond can accommodate more than 8 electrons around the central atom, allowing expanded octets like in SF6 and PCl5.

quiz.q: What determines whether a covalent bond is polar or nonpolar?
o: The difference in electronegativity between the bonded atoms
The number of lone pairs on each atom
The overall charge of the molecule
quiz.e: Bond polarity is determined by the electronegativity difference between the two bonded atoms; larger differences mean more polar bonds.

quiz.q: Which best describes why ionic compounds have high melting points?
o: Strong electrostatic attractions throughout the crystal lattice require large amounts of energy to break
Ionic compounds have weak intermolecular forces
Ionic compounds are always gases at room temperature
Ionic bonds involve electron sharing, which is weak
quiz.e: The strong, extended electrostatic (Coulombic) attractions between oppositely charged ions in a lattice require substantial energy to overcome, giving ionic solids high melting points.

quiz.q: What is the molecular geometry of a molecule with 6 electron domains and 2 lone pairs on the central atom?
quiz.e: With 6 domains and 2 lone pairs (typically placed opposite each other), the molecular shape is square planar (e.g. XeF4).

quiz.q: Which best describes why graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not, even though both are network covalent forms of carbon?
o: Graphite has delocalized pi electrons across its layers, while diamond's electrons are all localized in sigma bonds
Diamond has more valence electrons than graphite
quiz.e: Graphite's layered structure has delocalized electrons in pi bonds that can move freely within each layer, allowing conductivity; diamond's electrons are all localized in strong sigma bonds.

quiz.q: What is the approximate bond angle in a trigonal planar molecule like BF3?
quiz.e: Trigonal planar electron-domain geometry (3 domains, no lone pairs) gives ideal bond angles of 120 degrees.

quiz.q: Which molecule would you expect to have the highest boiling point due to intermolecular forces?
quiz.e: NH3 can hydrogen bond (H bonded to N), giving it stronger intermolecular forces and a higher boiling point than the other nonpolar/weakly polar molecules listed.

quiz.q: In the Lewis structure of SO2, what best explains the observed bond lengths, which are equal and intermediate between single and double bonds?
o: Resonance: the true structure is a hybrid of two resonance structures, each with one single and one double S-O bond
quiz.e: SO2 has two equivalent resonance structures; the actual molecule is an average (resonance hybrid), giving both S-O bonds equal, intermediate bond length and order.

quiz.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in CO2 (a linear molecule)?
quiz.e: CO2's carbon has 2 electron domains (2 double bonds, no lone pairs), corresponding to sp hybridization and a linear shape.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most likely be a nonpolar molecule despite containing polar bonds?
quiz.e: PCl5 is symmetric (trigonal bipyramidal, no lone pairs, identical terminal atoms), so its polar P-Cl bond dipoles cancel, making the molecule nonpolar overall.

quiz.q: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not as solids?
o: Ions become free to move and carry charge only when the rigid lattice breaks down (molten) or ions are separated (dissolved)
Ionic solids never conduct electricity under any conditions
Solid ionic compounds have delocalized electrons
Water reacts chemically with the ions to create new conductive species
quiz.e: In the solid lattice, ions are fixed in place and cannot move to carry current; melting or dissolving frees the ions to migrate and conduct electricity.

quiz.q: Which best explains why boiling point generally increases going down the halogens (F2, Cl2, Br2, I2)?
o: Increasing number of electrons increases the strength of London dispersion forces
The bonds within each molecule get weaker
quiz.e: As atomic/molecular size and electron count increase down the halogen group, London dispersion forces strengthen, raising boiling point despite these molecules being nonpolar.

quiz.q: What is the term for a solid, like ice, that is held together primarily by intermolecular hydrogen bonds between discrete molecules?
quiz.e: Ice consists of discrete H2O molecules held in a lattice by hydrogen bonds (an intermolecular force), classifying it as a molecular solid.

quiz.q: Which statement about bond order and bond strength/length is correct?
o: Higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond
Higher bond order means a longer, weaker bond
Bond order has no relationship to bond length
Bond order only applies to ionic bonds
quiz.e: As bond order increases (single to double to triple), bonds become shorter and require more energy to break (stronger).

quiz.q: Which type of solid would be expected to be brittle, have a high melting point, and NOT conduct electricity as a solid but conduct when molten?
quiz.e: Ionic solids are hard and brittle with high melting points; the ions are fixed in the solid lattice (no conduction) but become mobile and conduct when melted.

quiz.q: Which best describes the shape of a molecule with 5 electron domains: 3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs?
quiz.e: With 5 domains and 2 lone pairs occupying equatorial positions, the resulting molecular shape is T-shaped (e.g. ClF3).

quiz.q: Why does NF3 have a smaller dipole moment than NH3, even though F is more electronegative than H?
o: The individual N-F bond dipoles point opposite to the lone pair's contribution, partially canceling the molecular dipole, unlike in NH3
NF3 has no lone pair on nitrogen
F atoms cannot form polar bonds
quiz.e: In NF3, the highly electronegative F atoms pull electron density away from N in a direction that partially opposes the lone pair's dipole contribution, reducing the net molecular dipole compared to NH3.

quiz.q: What best describes the difference between a sigma bond and a pi bond?
o: A sigma bond forms from direct end-to-end orbital overlap along the bond axis; a pi bond forms from sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis
A sigma bond is always weaker than a pi bond
Pi bonds can exist without a sigma bond in the same connection
Sigma and pi bonds are identical in strength and orientation
quiz.e: Sigma bonds form via head-on orbital overlap along the internuclear axis; pi bonds form via sideways overlap of parallel unhybridized p orbitals, occurring only in double/triple bonds alongside a sigma bond.

quiz.q: Which best explains why CH4 (nonpolar) has a much lower boiling point than H2O (polar) despite CH4 having a larger molar mass?
o: Water's hydrogen bonding provides much stronger intermolecular attraction than CH4's London dispersion forces alone
quiz.e: Even though CH4 has a slightly larger molar mass, it lacks any dipole or hydrogen bonding and relies solely on weak London dispersion forces, giving it a far lower boiling point than hydrogen-bonded water.

quiz.q: What is the correct number of electron domains around the central atom in ClF5?
quiz.e: Chlorine forms 5 bonds to F and retains 1 lone pair, giving 6 total electron domains and a square pyramidal molecular shape.

quiz.q: Why is the O-H bond in water considered polar covalent rather than ionic?
o: The electronegativity difference between O and H, while significant, is not large enough to fully transfer the electron; electrons are still shared, just unequally
Oxygen and hydrogen have identical electronegativities
Hydrogen and oxygen are both nonmetals, so the bond must be ionic
Water has no bond polarity at all
quiz.e: An electronegativity difference around 1.4 (O-H) is large enough to create significant bond polarity but not large enough for a full electron transfer, keeping it polar covalent rather than ionic.

quiz.q: Which best describes why noble gases have such low boiling points despite having many electrons in larger atoms like xenon?
o: Even though larger noble gases have stronger London dispersion forces than smaller ones, all noble gases still only have London dispersion forces (no permanent dipole), keeping boiling points relatively low compared to polar or hydrogen-bonded substances
Noble gases have strong ionic bonds
Noble gases have covalent network structures
quiz.e: As monatomic species with full octets, noble gases can only interact via London dispersion forces; despite this force strengthening with size, it remains weaker than dipole-dipole or hydrogen bonding, keeping their boiling points comparatively low.

quiz.q: Which best describes why SF6 can exist (an expanded octet) while OF6 cannot?
o: Sulfur (period 3) can accommodate more than 8 electrons around it, while oxygen (period 2) is limited to an octet
Oxygen is too electronegative to bond with fluorine
Sulfur has fewer valence electrons than oxygen
quiz.e: Only period 3 and beyond elements can expand their octet due to their larger size and additional accessible orbitals; period 2 elements like oxygen are strictly limited to 8 electrons.

quiz.q: For the reaction 2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g), doubling [NO] quadruples the rate, while doubling [O2] doubles the rate. What is the rate law?
quiz.e: Rate quadrupling (2^2) when [NO] doubles means order 2 in NO; rate doubling (2^1) when [O2] doubles means order 1 in O2, giving rate = k[NO]^2[O2].

quiz.q: What is the overall reaction order for the rate law rate = k[A]^2[B]?
quiz.e: Overall order is the sum of individual orders: 2 (in A) + 1 (in B) = 3.

quiz.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 seconds. What fraction of the original reactant remains after 60 seconds?
quiz.e: 60 seconds is 3 half-lives (60/20=3); remaining fraction = (1/2)^3 = 1/8.

quiz.q: Which graph would be linear for a first-order reaction?
quiz.e: The integrated first-order rate law is ln[A] = ln[A]0 - kt, so ln[A] vs. time gives a straight line with slope -k.

quiz.q: What effect does a catalyst have on a reaction's rate and mechanism?
o: It lowers the activation energy by providing an alternate pathway, increasing rate without being consumed
It shifts the equilibrium toward products
It is consumed in the reaction
quiz.e: A catalyst provides an alternate reaction pathway with lower activation energy, speeding up the reaction without being permanently consumed.

quiz.q: In a proposed two-step mechanism, step 1 (slow) is A + B -> C, and step 2 (fast) is C + A -> D. What is the predicted rate law?
quiz.e: The rate law is based on the rate-determining (slowest) step; step 1 is elementary, so rate = k[A][B].

quiz.q: For the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) <-> 2NH3(g), what is the correct Keq expression?
quiz.e: Keq = [products]^coeff / [reactants]^coeff = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3).

quiz.q: If Q < K for a reaction not at equilibrium, which direction will the reaction shift?
quiz.e: When Q < K, there are proportionally too few products, so the reaction shifts forward to increase products and reach K.

quiz.q: According to Le Chatelier's principle, what happens to the equilibrium position of an exothermic reaction if temperature is increased?
quiz.e: For an exothermic reaction, heat is treated as a product; adding heat (increasing T) shifts equilibrium toward the reactants (endothermic reverse direction), decreasing K.

quiz.q: Which disturbance actually changes the numerical value of K for a reaction?
quiz.e: Only a temperature change alters K; concentration and volume/pressure changes shift the equilibrium position but leave K unchanged, and catalysts don't affect K at all.

quiz.q: For a gas-phase equilibrium with more moles of gas on the product side, what happens if the container volume is decreased (pressure increased)?
o: Equilibrium shifts toward the reactants (fewer moles of gas)
Equilibrium shifts toward the products (more moles of gas)
quiz.e: Decreasing volume increases pressure; the system shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas to partially relieve that increased pressure.

quiz.q: What is true about a reaction with a very large Keq (Keq >> 1)?
o: At equilibrium, products are strongly favored over reactants
At equilibrium, reactants are strongly favored
The reaction has a very negative Delta H always
quiz.e: A large K means the products dominate at equilibrium relative to the remaining reactants.

quiz.q: What is an intermediate in a reaction mechanism?
o: A species produced in one step and consumed in a later step, not appearing in the overall equation
A species present at the start and end of the reaction
The species with the highest activation energy
quiz.e: Intermediates form during the mechanism and are consumed before the final products form, so they cancel out of the overall balanced equation.

quiz.q: A reaction has Delta G° = -50 kJ/mol. What can be concluded about its equilibrium constant K?
o: K is much greater than 1 (products favored)
K is much less than 1 (reactants favored)
K cannot be determined from Delta G°
quiz.e: Delta G° = -RTln(K); a very negative Delta G° corresponds to ln(K) being large and positive, meaning K >> 1.

quiz.q: Which statement about zero-order reactions is correct?
o: The rate is independent of reactant concentration
The rate is directly proportional to [A]
quiz.e: In a zero-order reaction, rate = k (a constant), independent of the reactant's concentration.

quiz.q: Why does percent ionization of a weak acid increase as the solution is diluted?
o: Le Chatelier's principle favors more dissociation as total concentration decreases relative to water, shifting equilibrium toward more ions
Dilution has no effect on ionization
Weak acids become strong acids when diluted
quiz.e: Dilution shifts the ionization equilibrium (HA <-> H+ + A-) forward per Le Chatelier's principle since the system responds to decreased ion concentration, increasing the percent ionized even though Ka stays constant.

quiz.q: What best describes the rate-determining step of a multistep mechanism?
o: The slowest step, which controls the overall observed rate
The last step in the mechanism
The step that produces the final product
quiz.e: The rate-determining step is the slowest elementary step, acting as a bottleneck that sets the pace for the whole reaction.

quiz.q: For a first-order reaction, if the rate constant k = 0.0693 s^-1, what is the half-life?
Which condition describes a system truly at chemical equilibrium?
o: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, and concentrations remain constant over time
All reactants have been converted to products
quiz.e: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse rates are equal (dynamic, not static), so net concentrations stop changing even though the reaction continues in both directions.

quiz.q: How does increasing temperature generally affect the rate constant k of a reaction?
o: It increases k because more molecules have energy exceeding Ea
It has no effect on k
It only affects k for endothermic reactions
quiz.e: Higher temperature increases the fraction of molecules with kinetic energy above the activation energy, increasing the rate constant k (per the Arrhenius equation).

quiz.q: A reaction is second order overall and first order in each of two reactants, A and B. If both [A] and [B] are tripled, by what factor does the rate increase?
quiz.e: rate = k[A][B]; tripling both gives (3)(3) = 9 times the original rate.

quiz.q: What does a plot of 1/[A] vs. time being linear indicate about a reaction?
o: The reaction is second order in A
The reaction is first order in A
The reaction is zero order in A
The reaction has no defined order
quiz.e: The integrated second-order rate law, 1/[A] = 1/[A]0 + kt, produces a straight line when 1/[A] is plotted against time.

quiz.q: Which best describes the role of a reaction intermediate versus a catalyst in a mechanism?
o: An intermediate is produced then consumed within the mechanism; a catalyst is consumed early and regenerated later
Both intermediates and catalysts appear in the overall balanced equation
A catalyst is produced then consumed; an intermediate is regenerated
There is no difference between the two
quiz.e: Intermediates are formed in one step and used up in a later step; catalysts are present at the start (consumed in an early step) and regenerated in a later step, so they aren't net consumed.

quiz.q: For the equilibrium 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <-> 2SO3(g), which change would increase the value of Keq (assuming the forward reaction is exothermic)?
quiz.e: For an exothermic forward reaction, decreasing temperature shifts equilibrium toward products and actually increases the numerical value of K, unlike volume or catalyst changes.

quiz.q: If a reaction has Delta G° = 0, what can be said about K?
quiz.e: Delta G° = -RTln(K); if Delta G° = 0, then ln(K) = 0, so K = 1.

quiz.q: Which of the following would NOT shift the position of a gas-phase equilibrium?
o: Adding an inert (noble) gas at constant volume
Increasing the concentration of a reactant
quiz.e: Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change the partial pressures or concentrations of the reacting species, so it has no effect on the equilibrium position.

quiz.q: A reaction has a rate law of rate = k[A]. If [A] is doubled, what happens to the initial rate?
quiz.e: For a first-order dependence on A, rate is directly proportional to [A], so doubling [A] doubles the rate.

quiz.q: What best describes the relationship between a large activation energy (Ea) and reaction rate at a given temperature?
o: A large Ea generally corresponds to a slower reaction, since fewer molecules have enough energy to react
A large Ea always makes a reaction faster
Ea has no effect on reaction rate
A large Ea means the reaction is exothermic
quiz.e: A higher activation energy means fewer collisions have sufficient energy to react, resulting in a slower rate at a given temperature.

quiz.q: In an ICE table for the reaction A <-> B + C starting with only A present, if x moles of A react per liter, what is the equilibrium concentration of A?
quiz.e: As the reaction proceeds forward, A is consumed, so its equilibrium concentration is the initial concentration minus the amount reacted, x.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes how a system reaches equilibrium if it starts with pure reactants?
o: The forward rate starts high and decreases, the reverse rate starts at zero and increases, until they become equal
The forward and reverse rates are equal from the start
The reaction stops once any product forms
The reverse rate is always greater than the forward rate
quiz.e: Initially only the forward reaction can occur; as products build up, the reverse rate increases while the forward rate (limited by decreasing reactant) decreases, until the two rates equalize at equilibrium.

quiz.q: Which best explains why increasing surface area of a solid reactant increases reaction rate?
o: More particles are exposed and available for collisions with other reactants
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction
It increases the concentration of the solid
It changes the reaction's rate law order
quiz.e: Greater surface area exposes more reactant particles to collide with other reactants, increasing collision frequency and thus rate, without changing Ea or the rate law itself.

quiz.q: A reaction's rate doubles for every 10°C rise in temperature. If the rate at 20°C is 0.05 M/s, what is the rate at 40°C?
quiz.e: A 20°C rise is two 10°C increments, so the rate doubles twice: 0.05 x 2 x 2 = 0.20 M/s.

quiz.q: For an elementary bimolecular step A + B -> products, what is the rate law for that step?
quiz.e: For an elementary step, the rate law can be written directly from its molecularity/stoichiometry: rate = k[A][B].

quiz.q: Which observation would be strong evidence that a reaction has reached equilibrium?
o: The concentrations of reactants and products stop changing over time even though the reaction is still occurring
The temperature of the system stops changing
quiz.e: A constant Q (matching K) with unchanging concentrations, while the forward and reverse reactions continue, is the hallmark of dynamic equilibrium.

quiz.q: Why does a catalyst not appear in the overall balanced chemical equation?
o: It is regenerated by the end of the mechanism, so it is not consumed overall
It has no chemical role in the mechanism
It only affects physical properties, not chemistry
quiz.e: A catalyst participates in an early mechanistic step but is regenerated in a later step, so it has no net change and does not appear in the overall equation.

quiz.q: Which factor does NOT appear directly in the Arrhenius equation, k = Ae^(-Ea/RT)?
quiz.e: The Arrhenius equation relates rate constant k to activation energy, temperature, and the frequency factor — it does not include the equilibrium constant K.

quiz.q: If Kc for a reaction at a given temperature is 4.0 x 10^-8, what can be concluded?
o: The reaction strongly favors reactants at equilibrium
The reaction strongly favors products at equilibrium
The reaction is at equilibrium already regardless of concentrations
quiz.e: A very small K (<<1) means that at equilibrium, reactant concentrations dominate over product concentrations.

quiz.q: For a reaction with negative Delta H and positive Delta S, under what temperature conditions is it spontaneous?
quiz.e: Delta G = Delta H - TDelta S; with Delta H negative and Delta S positive, Delta G is negative at every temperature, making the reaction always spontaneous.
